title: WIP: Qt: Add dark mode profile support.
description:
Add a "Dark Mode" profile along with logic to switch between it and the
default profile when needed. Closes #15511.

Add a script that converts the default colorfilters file to a dark one.

Reverse our "marked" and "follow" colors in dark mode.

milestone.title: Wireshark release 4.0
milestone.description:
Issues and merge requests for the 4.0.0 release, which is currently unscheduled. Major changes include:

* Dropping support for 32-bit Windows.
* Shipping our Windows and macOS packages with Qt 6.
* Display filter syntax fixes and enhancements.
* Conversation UI updates.
* Various build requirement updates.

notes.body: Copying over https://code.wireshark.org/review/#/c/35142/ from Gerrit. I'm not sure if this should be merged in its current state, but it fixes filter syntax readability for me here.

I don't like this change for the reasons I had in Gerrit:
> I don't really like the idea to have Light Mode and Dark Mode specific profiles. I want to be able to use all my profiles both in Light and Dark mode. Latest macOS has a Auto Mode which will select mode according to time of day, and using this mode would require double of all profiles (on light and one dark).
What about "Light" and "Dark" tabs in Coloring rules and for the Colors part of "Preferences -> Appearance -> Font and Colors"? This way the user can configure specific settings for both modes. For coloring rules the list should have the same rules just with equal or different fg/bg colors.
Is it possible to automatically make a dark mode coloring rule from a light mode by "inverting" the colors?

I haven't tested this exact MR, but I wrote this in Gerrit:
> I briefly tried this change and I found some issues:
> 1. Starting with Default profile will switch to a "Dark Mode" profile, but this does not exist and is not listed in the lower right popup or the Configuration Profiles dialog (only the global is listed but not selected). Usually when selecting a global profile this is copied to a personal profile.
> 2. The Dark Mode colorfilters file is not used when the automatic profile switch occurs. Switching profiles a few times fixes this. Maybe related to 1.
> 3. "Marked" colors are not changed, but "Ignored" colors are changed.
> 4. The other prefs.* colors does not change correctly when switching profile or switching Light/Dark Mode.

Also, profiles are used for a lot more than coloring rules, and a user not using profiles will find issues with their other preferences and settings when the Default profile is automatically switched when changing to Light or Dark mode.

![image](/uploads/17918d9cecca1293a3d77ff58373d871/image.png)

I am trying a new approach, that will work without a profile. To be quite honest, this is a test-balloon based on this project:

https://github.com/Jorgen-VikingGod/Qt-Frameless-Window-DarkStyle

I have tested my code on Windows so far and it seems to work in nearly all cases (except where our graph library is painting e.g. IOGraph, but I am certain that I can find a solution for that). Testing on Mac and Linux is still out, but I can switch between layouts and designs. If I add some glue code, we might even be able to avoid implementing a class per theme and rather have JSON/qss files, which would enable users to theme their installation without us providing themes, similar to profiles (or the theme could be included in a profile, but that goes against the boundaries, mentioend by @stigbjorlykke above).

From what I can see from my testing so far, this works actually pretty well on Windows without that many adaptions. But I am judging from a default state of 3.7 here, not played around with colors much in the past.

And as you can see, the PacketList window also does not apply the theme yet, but I have to say, that might not even be a dealbreaker. I will look into it though and with a little tweek that might work as well.

Some more screenshots from dialogs. Notice, the titlebar is not yet properly adapted. And also, the open/save dialogs, as those are pretty custom.

![image](/uploads/d3cb0aea61aa237435ef8a1eda8ddcbf/image.png)
![image](/uploads/2aec5a76ad28bee3e0bc7359b3b26078/image.png)
![image](/uploads/be571520dcb5d50132f34853817561d0/image.png)
This looks great! The open and save dialogs are native on Windows. We might be able to fix their behavior with https://github.com/ysc3839/win32-darkmode.

I opened a new thread/merge request for the change. It just seemed more appropriate. (see !6382) 

I looked at the win32-darkmode. I will omit the file dialogs for now as I think this might be a slight overkill and also I want a more centralistic approach using Qt. I will take a look if it cannot achieved simply with "styling" using the qss styles.
mentioned in issue #18246

I agree with Stig on this; profiles should be independent of systematic GUI preferences such as light/dark mode.  Whether the user wants Wireshark to be dark-on-light or light-on-dark is orthogonal to whether the user is currently looking at an 802.11 capture or an Ethernet capture or a {pick your flavor of mobile data} capture or....

Either we should store both light mode and dark mode coloring profiles, or should store one coloring profile and algorithmically convert it to the "other" mode.

It may be that no algorithmic conversion is good enough that nobody would want to tweak its results, in which case storing both (e.g., "colorfilters" and "colorfilters-dark" in the profile's directory), and having the Coloring Rules dialog edit the appropriate one for the current display mode, and save to the other one with added rules saved with the colors converted algorithmically, deleted rules not saved, and modified rules saved with the colors converted algorithmically (and unchanged rules saved as they were in the file before the change), might be the right answer.

> (e.g., "colorfilters" and "colorfilters-dark" in the profile's directory)

...which raises the question of what to do if the user's manually edited one of them but not the other.

Another possibility would be to define a new file format for coloring rules, with the line for the rule containing both light-mode and dark-mode colors.  The file in the new format could be called "coloringrules" (to match what we call its contents, and what its contents are), and we could read it by default and, if there isn't a coloringrules file but there is a colorfilters file, read the colorfilters file and algorithmically convert the colors.  Coloring rules would be saved to the coloringrules file, with the colorfilters file written out with the light-mode colors for the benefit of older releases.
What about other colors from Preferences > Font and Colors?

I think we should keep the "colorfilters" file and extend it to support four colors, and use an algorithm to compute the dark-mode colours when missing. This will ensure old and new profiles will work on old and new Wireshark. Personally I like the algorithm to switch fg and bg colors.

When editing in UI I think the user should edit the colors in the current mode. When adding a new rule the other mode should be generated until changed by the user. Optionally we could add a button to switch the list from light-mode to dark-mode colors for easier editing. When using only one appearance mode one should not be bothered with colors for the other mode. A second option can be to lock the rules to only use light-mode or dark-mode colors regarding of system mode.

The Fonts and Colors preferences should be similar, generate the dark-mode colors and let user change in the same way as colorfilters. The dark-mode color probably need new "gui.*frame.[fb]g" entries, unless a magic delimiter can be used to avoid a syntax error.

I/O Graphs should also be similar, with an option to show the graph in light-mode or dark-mode. The dark-mode color can be added last to the "io_graphs" file.

Do we have other user configurable colors?

I strongly disagree on this approach. Switching fg/bg is an old-style color mode and not really applicable to modern UIs. Also, this will lead to scenarios, where Wireshark will break consistency with the rest of the system, as it will look vastly different compared to other apps. 

Additionally, I also do not think that we should further go down the road of color filters for UI. The color filters should apply to the dissection only, and dark mode can be calculated by calculating the offset , without having the need to store a specific dark mode profile. There already exist algorithms doing exactly that, and for the user it will be reversible, no matter if he changed the dark or light color.

The underlying problem is neither solved by this change nor by storing the preference in the profile though. The underlying problem is, that we do not apply and use the Qt style system correctly, but rather implement our own. To do this right, we should abandon this approach and move to the Qt style system (except for the coloring of our results). This would allow us to have a much cleaner configuration and for the end-user a much better integration into the rest of the system. I also do not see the necessity for a compatibility in such a case, as it would be adapting a system to a new one, abandoning a 25year old approach. Obviously this would mean, that it would be a major-version change, making it 5.x as the earliest.

Sorry, I should refrain of writing complex posts after too few hours of sleep due to the kids. What I meant is, that colorfilters should strictly apply to content we directly control, aka the packet-list, the packet details, byte view, iograph, ... 

For everything else, we should apply the system-wide styles. This is mostly how we do things. Mostly, but sadly not completely. Also, previously Qt5 had no method to correctly identify theme switches on all platforms, and Qt up to 6.4 also does not really do a great job. They are starting to integrate that into Qt just now.

What I am opposed is, to set a specific color for both modes. I think most users will stick with either mode, and therefore it would make sense to set only a color for reference and calculate the vice versa one? But that is a personal opinion, and I am well aware, that not everyone shares a similar view.

https://blog.zeplin.io/dark-mode-color-palette does a good job on explaining the issues with colors btw. It is a science in itself, and simply switching bg and fg would not lead to a good result in my opinion.

> colorfilters should strictly apply to content we directly control, aka the packet-list, the packet details, byte view, iograph, ...

It appears you are using the term "colorfilters" to apply to items other than the items that are contained in the "colorfilters" file, that are edited by View > Coloring Rules, and that consist of a set of colors and a packet-matching rule ("display filter") such that, for each packet in the packet summary pane, the colors of the first entry whose rule matches that packet will be applied to that packet, overriding whatever colors would otherwise be used.

If you are doing so, please choose some other term for this purpose, such as "user color settings"; the term "color filter" has a very specific meaning, and using it for any purpose other than to refer to the coloring rules causes confusion.

The packet list colors are affected by *two* user settings:

- the coloring rules;
- the "sample marked packet text" and "sample ignored pcket text" preferences in the Appearance > Font and Colors preference pane.

(There may be others that I have missed.)

The packet detail colors and the byte view colors are not, as far as I know, affected by any user settings.

The I/O Graph colors are selected by the user; the coloring rules don't affect them.

I have yet to see a suggestion that the coloring rules be used for any purpose other than coloring the packet list, so I see no need to worry about 
the color rules" applying to anything other than "the dissection".

> For everything else, we should apply the system-wide styles. This is mostly how we do things. Mostly, but sadly not completely.

So where are the cases where we do *not* apply the system-wide styles?

> I think most users will stick with either mode

macOS offers a *third* mode, "Auto", in which, to quote [Apple's documentation](https://support.apple.com/guide/mac-help/use-a-light-or-dark-appearance-mchl52e1c2d2), "Auto switches the appearance from light to dark based on the Night Shift schedule you set."  It would be a mistake to design our light/dark mode mechanism, at least in the macOS version of our software, around the assumption that people either go with light mode or dark mode, or that the people who don't do so don't matter.  Auto mode should Just Work.

It appears that Windows does not currently offer that, although a third-party app, [Auto Dark Mode](https://github.com/AutoDarkMode/Windows-Auto-Night-Mode), appears to do that.

I don't know whether the Big Two free-software desktops (GNOME and KDE) offer any form of time-dependent mode switching (assuming they even have a Big Switch to flip to go between light and dark mode).

> I don't know whether the Big Two free-software desktops (GNOME and KDE) offer any form of time-dependent mode switching (assuming they even have a Big Switch to flip to go between light and dark mode).

There are some [third party apps](https://wiki.archlinux.org/title/Dark_mode_switching) that do this. The Big Switch to flip all currently running apps on the fly (instead of just when launching a new app) works under GNOME and KDE (and non KDE-Qt apps), so long as you pick a theme that has a dark mode variant.

Yes you are correct, I am misusing the term. Used-defined colors makes more sense in the overall area of the project. We do use some of the defined colors and styles in other parts, but I think it applies more to the parts like font-size and weight than colors themselves. I think we will have to just see what is affected and try to correct it where easily possible.

I am aware of the auto setting, personally not using it but I know it exists. The issue is, what is being signaled. Windows for instance does in fact signal not a theme change but a color palette change, Apple signals a theme change. LSB and underlying mechanics would signal a theme change, which the major desktops as well as others (like Cinnamon or LxQt) adhere to as well, so it can be well assumed that it exists.

I will resolve this thread, I raised my point - although a little bit confusing - and I will raise it again if it exists after changes yet to be implemented or decided on.

> Windows for instance does in fact signal not a theme change but a color palette change,

From the Windows 11 dialog, which offers "Custom" in addition to "Light" an d "Dark", and from [the Microsoft documentation](https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/change-colors-in-windows-d26ef4d6-819a-581c-1581-493cfcc005fe), I'm not sure it has a notion of a two-position light vs. dark switch, it just has a changeable color palette, with "Light", "Dark", and "Custom" being three settings for the palette, and the ability for the user to change some colors in the palette in each of the settings, with the settings that can be changed differing between the three settings.

> Apple signals a theme change

Apple doesn't offer much of an editable color palette (that's somewhat Appleish nnot to do so).  In Ventura, you can change the "accent color" to either "multicolor" (which I think means "let the application pick its own accent color") or one of a set of Apple-chosen colors, and you can change the "highlight color" to either "Accent color" (meaning the accent color, which could mean "the application's accent color" if "accent color" was set to "multicolor") or one of a set of Apple-chosen colors.

My color sense is not a delicate as was Steve "hey, Google, you didn't get the right color for the second 'o' in your logo in your iOS app" Jobs, especially at my age, but the accent and highlight colors might not change in light and dark mode - or maybe a choice of "blue" or "yellow", for example, chooses one version of blue for light mode and another version for dark mode.

I'm not sure what Apple signals if the "accent color" or "highlight color" is changed.

> LSB and underlying mechanics would signal a theme change, which the major desktops as well as others (like Cinnamon or LxQt) adhere to as well, so it can be well assumed that it exists.

I think the free software desktops implement light and dark mode by having dark versions of themes (or, rather, by assuming that a theme might have a dark version - the naming convention might be "<theme name>-dark"), so "theme change" means "completely new theme selected".

I'm thinking about configuring the coloring rules like this for each profile. The user will have the same rules in both tabs, but with different colors. Adding a rule in one list will also add the rule in the other list. The user can then choose to edit the colors in both tabs, or keep them the same. The profiles shipped with Wireshark will have both lists adapted for light and dark mode.

Is this still relevant?
The comments contain lots of valuable information, but the change itself doesn't appear to be the right approach. Closing.

+/*
+ * Each line in the colorfilters file has the following format:
+ *
+ * @<filter name>@<filter string>@[<background>][<foreground>]
+ * Background and foreground colors are 16-bit comma-separated RGB
+ * triplets.
+ *
+ * To do:
+ * - Support a more standard, copy+paste-able color scheme, e.g.

+ */
+

 #define BLUE_COMPONENT(x)  (guint16) ( (((x)        & 0xff) * 65535 / 255))

+#!/usr/bin/env python3
+#
+# darken-colorfilters.py - Convert the default colorfilters file to one
+# that conforms to a dark theme.
+#
+# Wireshark - Network traffic analyzer
+# By Gerald Combs <gerald@wireshark.org>
+# Copyright 2019 Gerald Combs
+#
+# SPDX-License-Identifier: GPL-2.0-or-later
+'''Generate `profiles/Dark Mode/colorfilters` from `colorfilters`.
+'''
+
+import io
+import os.path
+import re
+import sys
+
+def main():
+    if sys.version_info[0] < 3:
+        print("This requires Python 3")
+        sys.exit(2)
+
+    this_dir = os.path.dirname(__file__)
+    light_cf = os.path.join(this_dir, '..', 'colorfilters')
+    dark_cf = os.path.join(this_dir, '..', 'profiles', 'Dark Mode', 'colorfilters')
+
+    # @<filter name>@<filter string>@[<background>][<foreground>]
+    rule_re = re.compile('(^[^#].*)\[(\d+),(\d+),(\d+)\]\[(\d+),(\d+),(\d+)\]([\r\n]+)')
+    dm_lines = []
+    with io.open(light_cf, 'r', encoding='UTF-8') as light_fd:
+        for line in light_fd:
+            dark_line = None
+            m = rule_re.match(line)
+            threshold = 12000
+            if m:
+                rule = m.groups()[0]
+                (bg_r, bg_g, bg_b, fg_r, fg_g, fg_b) = [int(chan) for chan in m.groups()[1:7]]
+                end = m.groups()[7]
+                # The standard light mode foreground color is 4718,10030,11796.
+                if fg_r < threshold and fg_g < threshold and fg_b < threshold:
+                    dark_line = '{}[{},{},{}][{},{},{}]{}'.format(rule, fg_r, fg_g, fg_b, bg_r, bg_g, bg_b, end)
+
+            if dark_line:
+                dm_lines.append(dark_line)
+            else:
+                dm_lines.append(line)
+
+    with io.open(dark_cf, 'w', encoding='UTF-8') as dark_fd:
+        dark_fd.write(''.join(dm_lines))
+
+if __name__ == '__main__':
+    main()

commits_data.message:
WIP: Qt: Add dark mode profile support.

Add a "Dark Mode" profile along with logic to switch between it and the
default profile when needed. Closes #15511.

Add a script that converts the default colorfilters file to a dark one.

Reverse our "marked" and "follow" colors in dark mode.
